newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: West African gold miners smile as S.Africans sweat.
newsitem.headline: West African gold miners smile as S.Africans sweat.

text.p: West Africa's low-cost gold producers should weather the latest gold price plunge with ease while the giant South African gold industry prepares for huge losses and layoffs of thousands of miners, analysts said.
With gold at its lowest level in 12 years and sliding lower by the hour, South Africa's mining houses are preparing for an uncertain future.
"It could be the worst thing the country has ever seen. This gold crisis is the last thing the country needs right now," said an analyst who asked not to be named.

South African gold mines are already digging deeper under the surface than any mines in the world to reach dwindling ore deposits, and the weakening gold price could affect them severely. Analysts expected the first bad signs to surface during the quarterly reporting season due to start on Thursday.
"I think we are going to see a bloodbath in general," Mathison and Hollidge gold analyst Angus Auchterlonie said.
One exception might be Anglo American Corp of South Africa Ltd, which could win some respite through its forward sales of gold.

But West Africa's fast-emerging gold industry -- centred around Ghana's Ashanti Goldfields Co Ltd -- would hardly be affected by the low bullion price due to sophisticated hedging policies and low operating costs.

South Africa's gold industry -- the world's largest producer with 495 tonnes of gold last year -- dwarfs that of its nearest African rivals, Ghana, which produced 51 tonnes, and Zimbabwe with 26.7 tonnes in 1996.

Analysts said unlike South Africa's high-cost producers, most gold mines in West Africa produced gold at a cash cost well below the world average, estimated by Gold Fields Mineral Services to be $262 an ounce.
BOE Natwest analyst Barry Sergeant said the cash cost of most of the gold mines in West Africa was between $200 and $250.
Auchterlonie said if capital expenditure and the effects of hedging were excluded, only three South African mines had a cash operating cost of less than $250 an ounce.
Sergeant said Ashanti had the most successful forward sales policy of any gold producer on the African continent and could expect a spot gold price from hedging of more than $400.
"At Ashanti Goldfields right now it is just business as usual," Sergeant said.
Ashanti's corporate affairs manager, James Anaman, told Reuters by telephone from Ghana that the present bullion price would not affect the company in the short term.
"We have taken a very sophisticated attitude to the question of hedging and therefore we are fairly well covered in the short term certainly," Anaman said.
He said Ashanti should realise a spot price of $430 for 1997 through its forward sales.
The company had entered into contracts to deliver 982,000 ounces at a price of $426 an ounce in its 1997 financial year.

"Having said all that, as we say here in Ghana, it is a fool who says my neighbour's house is burning and is doesn't affect me. This affects the whole industry and is a big damper on the industry. It is sad to see other producers going down," Anaman said.

In Zimbabwe, some gold miners had already scaled down operations and cut jobs and the country's Chamber of Mines was negotiating with the government to introduce a floor price for local producers, Chamber chief executive Derek Bain said.
"The low gold price has left many companies in dire straits. We are still talking to the government on this issue which we see as one of the best ways to restore viability," he said.

But Sergeant and other analysts said the biggest impact of the fall in the gold price, following soon after the Bre-X Minerals scandal, would be on exploration in Africa -- where large areas are still to be explored by modern geological methods.
"There has definitely been a severe impact on exploration in the Pan-Africa area, firstly as a result of Bre-X and that has been aggravated by the gold price.
"For the exploration companies on the Pan-African stage which are not established, there has been a severe curtailment of funding that is impossible to quantify," Sergeant said.

Confidence in mining exploration was dented earlier this year after an Indonesian gold find touted by Canada's Bre-X Minerals Ltd as the biggest discovery this century was found to contain no commercially viable gold deposits.
